items.followUp: Using a velocity-time graph, derive the second equation of motion, s = ut + ½at².

rubric.why: The labelled velocity-time graph represents the body's initial and final velocities over time t.
rubric.description: Draws and labels the velocity-time graph for the motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a graph with velocity and time axes and the values u, v and t correctly shown.

rubric.why: The displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a trapezium.
rubric.description: Uses the area of the trapezium to express displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct area expression.

rubric.why: The acceleration relation gives time in terms of the velocities and acceleration, allowing time to be eliminated.
rubric.description: Uses the acceleration relation to eliminate time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct acceleration relation and expression for t.

rubric.why: This is the required third equation of motion.
rubric.description: Obtains the third equation of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final equation.

modelAnswer: Draw the velocity-time graph with time t on the horizontal axis and velocity on the vertical axis.
Mark the initial velocity u at time 0 and the final velocity v at time t; join the points (0, u) and (t, v) with a straight line.
The area under the graph is a trapezium, so displacement s = ½(u + v)t.
From the definition of acceleration, a = (v − u)/t, hence t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = (u + v)(v − u)/(2a).
Therefore, 2as = v² − u², and v² = u² + 2as.

items.followUp: A 0.4 kg body moves at 5 m s⁻¹ in a circle of radius 2 m. Find the centripetal force.

rubric.why: The radius must be converted from centimetres to metres; all three values are then in SI units.
rubric.description: Writes the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for m = 0.5 kg, r = 0.5 m and v = 3 m s⁻¹.

rubric.why: The centripetal-force formula relates mass, speed and radius.
rubric.description: States the formula for centripetal force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for F = mv²/r, or for F = ma together with a = v²/r.

rubric.why: The SI values are substituted correctly into the formula.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values into the formula.

rubric.why: The calculated centripetal force is 4.5 N.
rubric.description: Calculates and states the centripetal force with its unit.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for 4.5 N. Award 1 mark if 4.5 is correct but the unit is missing.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 0.5 kg, r = 50 cm = 0.5 m, v = 3 m s⁻¹.
Substitution: F = (0.5 kg)(3 m s⁻¹)²/(0.5 m).

items.followUp: A wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 × 10⁻⁶ m² extends by 1 × 10⁻³ m under a force of 20 N. Find its Young's modulus.

accept: ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain
rubric.why: Young's modulus is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition; the elastic-limit condition may be stated or understood.

rubric.why: These expressions provide the stress and strain used in deriving the formula.
rubric.description: Writes the relations for tensile stress and tensile strain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both correct relations.

rubric.why: Substituting the stress and strain expressions gives the formula for Young's modulus.
rubric.description: Derives the formula for Young's modulus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for obtaining Y = FL/(AΔL), with or without the intermediate step.

rubric.why: The SI unit of Young's modulus is the same as the unit of stress.
rubric.description: States the SI unit of Young's modulus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for N m⁻² or pascal (Pa).

modelAnswer: Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain, provided the material is within its elastic limit.
Tensile stress = F/A, where F is the applied force and A is the cross-sectional area.
Tensile strain = change in length/original length = ΔL/L.
The SI unit of Young's modulus is N m⁻², also called the pascal (Pa).
